messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Photographer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kiet's eyes still scanned the streets with a mix of habit and instinct, his photographer's gaze now forever intertwined with the hypervigilance that had kept him alive in combat. It was a year ago that he'd returned from deployment, but the memories of those months in the war zone remained more real than any other moment in his life. He could still recall the sound of gunfire, the smell of smoke and sweat, and the weight of his rifle in his hands. It started with small things – jumpiness at car backfires or screams of children playing – but soon Kiet found himself constantly on edge, unable to relax even when he was alone in his apartment. He'd try to focus on editing photos for hours, only to find his mind drifting back to the worst moments: the ambush that killed two of his squad members, the sounds of their cries still echoing in his ears. Taking risks had become a way for Kiet to feel something other than numbness and guilt. He'd drive recklessly, pushing speeds on deserted roads, or take unnecessary risks while shooting in abandoned buildings. It was as if he needed to test his own mortality, to prove that he was still alive. His friends and family worried about him, but Kiet couldn't explain why he felt drawn to danger – only that it made the memories recede for a little while. When memories did surface, they brought with them a tide of rage. He'd be in the middle of a shoot, camera in hand, when suddenly he'd see his squad leader's face, remember the sound of gunfire, and feel an overwhelming urge to smash everything around him. It was as if the past had reached out and grabbed him by the throat, leaving him gasping for air. Kiet tried to avoid triggers – loud noises, crowded places – but they seemed to lurk everywhere. He'd be walking through a market when a vendor's shout would send him spinning back into the chaos of combat. The memories were so vivid that he sometimes felt like he was reliving them all over again, his heart racing and palms slick with sweat. In quieter moments, Kiet couldn't shake the feeling that he didn't belong anywhere anymore. He'd grown up in a tight-knit Vietnamese-American community, but now even familiar faces seemed foreign to him. People's smiles and laughter grated on his nerves; he was certain they couldn't understand what he'd been through. He mistrusted everyone – friends, family, even himself. Kiet felt like he should have protected his squad members that day, that somehow it was all his fault. He replayed the events in his head, wondering if there was something – anything – he could have done differently. The weight of those 'what ifs' crushed him at times, leaving him feeling like a failure. Photography had been Kiet's passion before deployment, but now even that felt tainted by his experiences. He couldn't bear to take portraits of happy families or smiling children; it all seemed so superficial compared to the reality he'd witnessed. His camera gathered dust as Kiet struggled to find meaning in anything he did. It was a particularly brutal memory – one that had been triggered by a chance encounter with an old comrade – that finally made Kiet realize he needed help. He couldn't keep living like this, constantly looking over his shoulder, waiting for the next flashback or nightmare. As he sat in his darkened apartment, surrounded by the detritus of his own broken dreams, Kiet knew it was time to face whatever demons had taken up residence inside him. With a sense of trepidation and hope, Kiet picked up the phone and dialed the number for a local VA support group. For the first time in months, he allowed himself to imagine that maybe – just maybe – there was a way out of this darkness, and back into the light.
